en: Points of Controversy The Great Fifty The Nineteenth Chapter
The Discussion on Absolute Certainty:
Is there absolute certainty for an ordinary person (puthujjana)?
Yes, [they say].
The matricide is absolutely fixed; the patricide …pe… the murderer of an arahant …pe… the shedder of blood …pe…
Is one who causes a schism in the Saṅgha absolutely fixed [in destiny]?
One should not say so …pe….
Is there such a thing as an ordinary person (puthujjana) who is absolutely fixed [in destiny]?
“Yes.
“Could doubt arise in a person who is absolutely fixed?
“Yes.”
If doubt were to arise in a person who is absolutely fixed, then surely it should not be said:
"An ordinary person possesses absolute fixity.
Is it not the case that doubt does not arise in a person who is absolutely fixed?
“Yes. “Is it abandoned?
“One should not say so … [and so on] …”
Is it abandoned?
Yes. Is it by means of the path of stream-entry? Yes.
It should not be stated thus … [and so on] … by the path of once-returning … [and so on] … by the path of non-returning … [and so on].
"By the path of arahantship"?
One should not say so ...
[and so on] ... "By which path?"
"By means of an unwholesome path.
Is it to be said that an unwholesome path is leading out, leading to destruction, leading to enlightenment, and is without taints …pe… non-defiled?
It should not be so stated …pe…
Is it not the case that the unwholesome path is not leading to liberation …pe… and is subject to defilement?
Yes, it is.
If the unwholesome path is not conducive to deliverance … [and] is subject to defilement,
then surely it should not be said that “for a person who is absolutely fixed,
doubt has been abandoned by means of the unwholesome path.”
If it is admitted that the view of annihilationism could arise in a person fixed in the view of eternalism, then indeed, O friend, you should not say: [that such a thing is impossible].
“There is absolute certainty for the worldling.
If that is so, would it not follow that for a person fixed in the view of eternalism, the view of annihilationism could never arise?
Yes, [it would].
"Is it abandoned?
"One should not say so... [etc.
"...is it abandoned?"
“Yes,” [you say].
“Is it by means of the path of stream-entry?
You should not say so … [and so on] …
Is it by means of the path of once-returning …pe… by means of the path of non-returning …pe… or by means of the path of arahantship?
It should not be said so … [as before] … By which path?
By an unwholesome path.
The unwholesome path... [as before] ...Indeed, you should not say:
"For a person fixed in the view of eternalism, the view of annihilationism has been abandoned by means of the unwholesome path.
Would the view of eternalism arise for a person fixed in the view of annihilationism?
“Yes.
[The opponent asks: “If, for a person fixed in the view of annihilationism, the view of eternalism were to arise, then indeed you should not say:
‘There is absolute fixity for the worldling.’”
If a person is fixed in the view of annihilationism, would the view of eternalism not arise for them?
Yes. Has it been abandoned? No.
It should not be said thus … [as before] … “Is it abandoned? Yes.
Is it by the path of stream-entry?
One should not say so …pe… by the path of once-returning …pe…
“By the path of non-returning …pe… by the path of arhatship”?
One should not say so …pe….
“By what path? “By an unwholesome path.
[If you say] the path is unwholesome … [and so on] … surely it should not be said: [that the path is unwholesome].
“Is it not to be said that for a person fixed in the view of annihilationism, the view of eternalism has been abandoned by means of the unwholesome path?
Is it not to be said that there is absolute fixity for a worldling?
“Yes, [he does].
“But was it not said by the Blessed One:
‘Here, monks, a certain person is endowed with exclusively dark, unwholesome states; he remains sunk once he has gone under’?”
Is this indeed a sutta? Yes.
Therefore, it follows that there is absolute certainty for the worldling.
The Blessed One has said:
“Here, bhikkhus, a certain person is possessed of entirely black, unwholesome states;
he remains sunk once he has gone under. Having said this, does it follow from that reason that there is absolute certainty for a worldling?
“Yes,
it was said by the Blessed One:
‘In this case, monks, a certain person, having emerged, sinks back down.’”
Is that indeed the Sutta? Yes.
Does it emerge and submerge at all times? No.
It should not be said thus… [as before]… It was said by the Blessed One:
“Here, monks, a certain person is possessed of entirely black unwholesome states; having once sunk down, he remains sunk.”
And for that reason, is it the case that there is absolute certainty for a worldling?
Yes, it is.
It was said by the Blessed One:
“Here, monks, a certain person, having emerged, stands; having emerged, he looks about with insight; having emerged, he crosses over; having emerged, he reaches a firm footing.
Is this indeed a sutta?
Yes, it is.
"Does one, having emerged at all times, reach a firm footing?
One should not say so... [etc.
...The Discussion on Absolute Certainty is finished.
